To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there is a certain capacity of microbial populations to maintain high levels of biodegradation function in response to recurrent disturbances; (ii) if this capacity is exceeded, the biodegradation function can still be maintained, but spatial zones of different performance develop; (iii) the biodegradation performance is enhanced by spatially fragmented disturbances; (iv) bacterial dispersal networks can facilitate functional resistance against recurrent disturbance, but lead to a decrease of bacterial biomass.

(1) the spatial distribution of disturbances determines the response of a microbial community to recurrent disturbances, and (2) functional resistance to recurrent disturbances can be enhanced by the activity of surviving bacteria in the core of the disturbed areas.

(i) Functional resistance to recurrent disturbances of biodegradation function is possible in a spatially heterogeneous ecosystem, (ii) this resistance can be facilitated by the formation of spatial dispersal networks that allow for reactivation of disturbed areas, and (iii) the bacterial biomass abundance in the system is not necessarily a good indicator of the biodegradation performance of the system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional resistance of ecosystems to disturbances.

functional resistance against disturbances is not necessarily associated with an increase in the bacterial biomass, but can also occur in a bacterial community with reduced overall biomass.
